title.en: Isigaligarssik and the Wizard Who Took His Wife
title.zh: 伊西加利加舒克與奪妻之巫

region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Isigaligarssik', eBook #28932

summary.en: The wifeless strongman Isigaligarssik weds the widow's daughter during a spirit-calling, but the jealous wizard banishes the marriage by the ritual of drying her shoes on the frame. When Isigaligarssik finally answers the taunt 'what of you who took my wife away?', the wizard stabs him; the wound heals the moment his childhood dress, dipped in water, touches it. In the bow-duel he shrinks himself to a nodding head, breaks the wizard's arrows, and kills him as he creeps into his passage way.
summary.zh: 無妻壯漢伊西加利加舒克在降靈夜娶得寡婦之女，妒巫卻以晾鞋之術斷其姻緣。他終於回罵『你奪我妻又如何』，巫師以刀重創其身；小時舊衣浸水觸傷即癒。弓箭決鬥中，他縮得只剩點動的頭顱，折斷巫箭，待其彎身入甬道時一箭射殺，奪回妻子。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Spirit-calling seance described as historical community practice.

passages.text: Isigaligarssik, a wifeless man and very strong, was taken to live with a house of brothers who were fond of him. The village wizard's custom at spirit-callings was to call through the window, 'Only the married men may come and hear,' so the little widow, her daughter, and Isigaligarssik always stayed behind. One evening the daughter whispered to her mother, who said: 'This little girl would like to have you.' Before the others returned they were man and wife. Next evening the rule reversed: 'Let only those who have wives come and hear' — and the great wizard, calling Isigaligarssik's wife to him, took off her shoes and hung them on the drying frame, a rite of banishment. After the calling he told Isigaligarssik: 'Go away now; you will never have this dear little wife of yours again.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Isigaligarssik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Every spirit-calling the wizard mocked him: 'Ho, what are you doing here, you who have no wife?' Anger grew slowly, and the village warned him — 'if you answer him, he will kill you.' One evening he answered: 'Ho, and what of you who took my wife away?' The wizard stood up at once, and as Isigaligarssik bent to creep out of the entrance, stabbed him with a great wound. Run home, he bade his wife's mother fetch from the chest the dress he wore when little, so small it hardly looked like a dress, and dip it in the water bucket; wet, it stretched enough to put on, and when the lacing thong at its hem touched the wound, it healed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Isigaligarssik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: His house-fellows, following the blood spoor after the calling, found him inside without a single wound and rejoiced. Next day he took from his chest a bow so small it could hardly be seen in his hands, challenged the wizard to a shooting match by the little river, and when the man aimed at him he made himself so small that only his head could be seen nodding. Twice the wizard shot and missed; Isigaligarssik stood, broke the arrow across, and said: 'Go home; you cannot hit.' And when the wizard, glancing back many times, bent to his passage way, Isigaligarssik aimed and shot — the little arrow doubled him up through the entrance, and he fell dead in the passage. So Isigaligarssik won his wife again and lived with her until death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Isigaligarssik'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Insects That Wooed a Wifeless Man

region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Insects that wooed a wifeless man', eBook #28932

summary.en: A chronically sleepy wifeless man saves a capsized kayaker — one of the Noseless Ones from beneath the earth — who grants him a single seal each dawn and forbids him ever to tell. Prosperity brings him a wife, but her questioning breaks the taboo; his luck dies, she leaves him through a rock crevice, and blowfly, fly, cranefly, centipede, and gnat each crawl out to woo him in turn. Reclaiming her, he is put under a sleeping spell and wakes to a summer-aged world: his kayak rotted through, years gone by.
summary.zh: 貪睡的無妻男子救起翻艇呼救者——地底無鼻族人——後者許其一晨一豹，且誡之不可外泄。富足為他娶得嬌妻，然而妻子追問破禁忌，獵運即盡；妻子自石隙離去，蒼蠅、大蚊、蜈蚣、蚊子逐一出洞求偶。他重新娶妻，卻陷入沉睡咒術，醒來時夏色滿地、皮艇朽爛，多年已逝。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The Noseless Ones are an otherworld people of Greenlandic oral cosmology.

passages.text: There was once a wifeless man — so every story begins — who was too sleepy to hunt, waking only at sunset when the kayakers came home with their catch. Rowing out one evening anyway, he heard a man crying that his kayak had upset, righted him, and saw he was one of the Noseless Ones, the people from beneath the earth. Refusing the reward of ornamented hide thongs — 'the only thing I cannot overcome is my miserable sleepiness' — he was led to land by the Fire Man, who announced him as the saviour of his life and laid down the terms: one beast and one only may you choose on your homeward way; be careful never to tell what you have seen, or it will go ill with your hunting hereafter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Insects that wooed a wifeless man'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Thenceforth the wifeless man went out before sunrise and came home with three seals while his fellows were still preparing to launch. The young girls who had once run from him now vied for his favour, laughing, and he chose the best of the flock. But his wife wearied of the endless cutting-up of seals and kept asking why he caught such a terrible lot. 'The seals come of themselves, and I catch them — that is all,' he said, until at last he told her everything: the capsized kayaker, the Noseless One, the gift. From that time forward he lost his power of hunting; the old sleepiness came over him, and he lost all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Insects that wooed a wifeless man'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Without even skins enough for her clothes, his wife ran away through a crevice in the rocks he could scarcely pass, and lay in wait inside. Out crawled a blowfly — 'Take me' — but he refused her: 'You pick your food from the muck-heaps.' Then a fly ('You lay your eggs about anyhow, and your eyes are quite abominably big'), a cranefly ('Your legs are too long'), a centipede ('Far too many legs... your eyes are simply nasty'), and a gnat ('No thanks, you bite') — each laughed and went back inside with the report. At last his wife bade him in, since he would have none of the others; he squeezed through the crack, took her to wife again, and asked her to comb his hair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Insects that wooed a wifeless man'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Combing, she sang over him: 'Do not wake until the fulmar begins to cry; sleep until we hear a sound of young birds.' He fell asleep — it was winter when he crawled in through the crack — and when he awoke the earth was blue with summer and the fulmar cried noisily on the bird cliff. His kayak down on the shore was rotted through with age. And he reached home, the teller says, and now sits scratching himself at ease. The tale folds the spirit-gift, the broken secrecy taboo, and the stolen time of the sleeping enchantment into one comic warning about a wifeless man and the wives of the insect world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Insects that wooed a wifeless man'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Very Obstinate Man Who Drove to the Moon

region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The very obstinate man', eBook #28932

summary.en: No one could be as obstinate as the Obstinate Man, who forces his mourning wife to sew his kayak cover — and the sewing raises a sea-monster dog, whose owner is the Moon Man. Wrestling the Moon Man nearly dead, he releases him only at the threat 'there will never be dawn or daylight again,' then follows the Moon Man's dog-team through the naked air. Warned to pass the great rock by its shady side, he goes by the sunny side and a knife-whetting old woman tears out his heart; retrieved and restored at the Moon, he watches his wife's evil thoughts rise as smoke, harpoons forbidden walrus from the sky, and comes home cured of his obstinacy.
summary.zh: 倔強無人能敵的男子強迫服喪中的妻子縫皮艇，縫線之聲竟喚出海中犬形怪物；其主乃月人。他扼喉幾乎勒死月人，直至對方喊出『再無黎明白晝』才罷手。他隨月人犬隊驅入長空，卻違囑繞行大石向陽一面，被磨刀老嫗挖去心臟；月人為其復心，又教他俯瞰人間——妻子惡念化煙——禁不住誘惑而叉獵天池海象。歸來後，他終於不再倔強。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Moon Man (tarraq) as sky regulator of tides and daylight is standard Greenlandic cosmology.

passages.text: There was once an Obstinate Man — no one in the world could be as obstinate as he, and no one dared come near him. When his wife lost her little child and sat idle at home in mourning, as the custom of the time required, he ordered her to sew the skin of his kayak down on the shore. Sewing, her thread began to make a sound, the sound a muttering, the muttering louder — and a monster in the shape of a dog rose out of the sea: 'Why are you sewing, you who are still in mourning?' The mighty dog sprang ashore upon the husband, but the Obstinate One would get his own way and killed the dog in the fight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The very obstinate man'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The dog's owner appeared — the Moon Man — and the Obstinate One fell upon him in turn, catching him by the throat, clenching until the Moon Man was nearly strangled. 'There will be no more ebb-tide or flood if you strangle me,' he cried; the Obstinate One clutched tighter. 'The seal will never breed again if you strangle me.' Tighter still. 'There will never be dawn or daylight again if you kill me' — at that the Obstinate One hesitated, for he did not like the thought of living in the dark forever, and let him go. The Moon Man called his dog to life, cast his team one by one up into the air until the whole sledge team hovered there, cracked his whip, and drove off through the naked air — but he invited the Obstinate One to visit him in the Moon, warning him: when you see a great rock in your way, drive round behind it; do not pass it on the sunny side, for your heart will be torn out of you.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The very obstinate man'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Obstinate One washed his dirt-caked dogs in the sea and cast them into the air until they stayed aloft, made a sledge, and drove off. At the rock he said to himself, 'Why should I drive round a rock at all? I will go by the sunny side.' Up alongside he heard a woman singing drum songs and whetting her knife, the steel humming; he tried to overpower the old woman and lost his senses, and when he came to himself, his heart was gone. Going round by the shady side, he came to the moon and told how he had lost it; the Moon Man laid him on his back on a black sealskin and stuffed the heart in again. From a lifted stone he looked down on the earth and saw his wife on the bench plaiting sinew before her mourning was passed, thick smoke — the smoke of her evil thoughts — rising from her body, and grew angry, forgetting that he himself had bidden her work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The very obstinate man'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Later the Moon Man opened a stone in the entrance and let him look down on a place full of walrus, lying one on top of another — 'It is a joy to catch such beasts.' Forbidden to harpoon, promised only a share of the Moon Man's own catch, the Obstinate One would not be content: he took harpoons from the store and, being a man of very great strength, killed one walrus on the line and then another. After his return from the Moon Man's place he left off being obstinate, and never again forced his wife to work while she was in mourning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The very obstinate man'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Dwarfs of the Deep Fjord

region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Dwarfs', eBook #28932

summary.en: A kayaker befriends a timid dwarf, carries up a seal with one hand to the amazement of the little folk, and wins the dwarf's mighty daughter in marriage. When the mixed family returns to the world of real people, a great black-and-white-faced dog devours the dwarf child in the passage; the terrified little folk flee from village to village, the old man hauling his tent-skins ashore to ask 'Are there any dogs here?' until the skin is worn from his forehead — and he calms a storm with a magic song about crested clouds in the clearing east.
summary.zh: 皮艇客結識羞怯的矮人，單手提豹上岸令小族驚為巨人，娶得矮人力大無窮的女兒。混居人間後，一隻黑白天面的大狗在甬道中吞食矮人幼兒；小族驚懼四逃，老翁每到一村便背著帳皮登岸問『此地有狗否？』，額頭皮膚為之磨穿——他更以一段『東天霽雲』的咒歌使怒海復平。狗吠聲起，他又倉皇登舟，飄然不知所終。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The storyteller performs the dwarf's part in a hurried jerky manner, per the source's note — performance convention documented here as context.

passages.text: A man out in his kayak rowed up to another kayak far off and found the paddler a very little man, a dwarf, plainly troubled and afraid. The dwarf said he was hunting a little fjord seal he could not hit; the stranger took his throw and struck it between the shoulder-blades — 'Ai, ai, what a throw!' cried the dwarf in astonishment. Rowing in company, the little one mumbled out his story in jerks: he had a daughter, very beautiful, whom many men wanted and could not take by force because she was too strong — even for her own father. 'Might perhaps do for you... you could manage her... what?' 'Let us first see her,' said the man, and they rowed into a great deep fjord.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Dwarfs'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the house of the little old man the guest's catch was cut up with heroic labour — the two women and the old man together could not drag the little seal up from the shore until the stranger carried it by one flipper; to the dwarfs, cutting it up was like cutting up a huge walrus, and each guest received a breastbone so large it reached to the ground. An old hag made herself agreeable and was frightened off with a loud whistle. Up in the other house the guest munched dried foxes' liver as if it were fresh meat while the dwarfs worked and could not cut it through. But the old man's daughter was the most beautiful, and he said he would have her to wife, and they lived happily and soon had a child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Dwarfs'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the man longed for his own kin, the whole dwarf family went with him to visit the world of real people, who were astonished to find their old comrade alive. The dwarf folk forgot to be afraid among the real men — until the little dwarf grandmother, sitting at the passage opening with the child, dropped it, and a great dog with a black face on one side and white on the other lay in the passage and ate it up on the spot. 'Nothing is left but a little smear on the ground,' she cried. The horror-stricken dwarf folk gathered their belongings and set out, and at every village the old man went ashore with his tent-skins on his back, asking first thing, 'Are there any dogs here? Is there a great beast with a black-and-white face?' — and at every yes he was back in his boat before anyone could turn round, until the skin was worn quite away from his forehead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Dwarfs'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, lying-to as a north wind began to blow, the old man groaned and asked his question — but heard the barking of the dogs themselves, and fled to his boat. The seas frothed white; then the old dwarf stood up in his boat and cried: 'The sky is clearing to the east with crested clouds.' It was a magic song: the sea was calm and bright at once, so great was the power of his words. But for all that he had no peace, by reason of the dogs, and went on his way again — and whither he came at last, the teller does not know.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Dwarfs'; not verbatim.
